title: Concurrency control: locks, deadlocks and SSI
goal: By the end you can explain why writers lock rows until commit, read `pg_locks` to see who waits for whom, find a deadlock as a cycle in a waits-for graph, say how SERIALIZABLE catches write skew without blocking readers, and build a lock manager that detects deadlocks.

warmup.q: In PostgreSQL, transfer A moves 12 euros from account 1 to account 2 while transfer B moves 8 euros from account 2 to account 1. Each first updates the account it takes money from, then the other one. What happens?
options: Both finish at once, because under MVCC writers never wait
Each waits for the other; after about a second PostgreSQL aborts one with a deadlock error, and the other finishes
Both wait until the connection pool's timeout fires
PostgreSQL notices the opposite order and runs B after A
warmup.why: A locks account 1 and B locks account 2; then each needs the row the other holds. That cycle can't end by itself. A waiting backend checks for cycles after `deadlock_timeout` (1 second by default) and aborts one transaction, so the other completes. The first option is the misconception lesson 7 corrected: readers don't block writers, but writers block writers. PostgreSQL never reorders your statements.

sections.h: Writers queue for locks, even under MVCC
sections.body:
Lesson 7 ended on a rule: readers don't block writers, but writers block writers. A refund and a capture that both change account 1 must take turns, or one change is lost. Lesson 7's store handled this bluntly: it failed the second writer with `WriteConflict` and left the retry to the application. That is wasteful when the first writer will be done in 2 ms. Waiting is better, and a **lock** is how a database makes a transaction wait for its turn.

Version 1 is one lock for the whole database, so only one transaction writes at a time. SQLite works like this: one writer at a time, while readers carry on in WAL mode. It is correct, but on a payments database with 300 transfers a second it makes every transfer wait for every other one, although two transfers rarely touch the same account.

Version 2 is a lock per row. A transfer locks the two accounts it changes, and transfers on other accounts never notice. Now a lock needs a mode. A transaction that only needs a row to stay unchanged while it checks something can share it with others doing the same: a shared lock (S), which `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` takes. A transaction that changes the row needs it alone: an exclusive lock (X), which every UPDATE and DELETE takes, and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` too. S is compatible with S. X is compatible with nothing.

A **lock manager** keeps, for every locked thing, who holds it and a queue of who waits for it. That is the figure, and the lab builds it. A request is granted if it is compatible with every holder and nobody is waiting ahead of it. The second condition is about fairness: without it, a steady stream of S requests could keep an X request waiting forever. When a holder releases, the lock manager grants waiting requests from the front of the queue, in order.

PostgreSQL has such a lock manager in shared memory, for tables and other objects. Row locks work differently, as lesson 7 showed: the lock is the locker's transaction id in the row's `t_xmax`, so locking a million rows costs no memory. To wait for a row, a transaction waits on the lock that every transaction holds on its own id until it ends. In the Try it, the second UPDATE of account 1 appears in `pg_locks` as a `ShareLock` request on transaction 858, not granted. It also holds a `tuple` lock on `(0,1)`, which marks its place in line for that row: a third writer would queue behind it.

try.title: Find the waiting transaction in pg_locks
steps: From `labs/`, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, then open two terminals in `labs/` and run `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz` in each: terminal 1 and terminal 2 below.
Terminal 1: create `accounts`, start a transaction that debits account 1, and note its pid and transaction id. Terminal 2: update account 1 too. It hangs.
Terminal 1: list the locks. Predict which row has `granted = f`, and which transaction id it names. Then commit and watch terminal 2 return.

code.title: two psql sessions

try.expect:
Terminal 1 is pid 128 with transaction 858, terminal 2 is pid 142:

```text
 pid |   locktype    |   rel    | page | tuple | xid |       mode       | granted
-----+---------------+----------+------+-------+-----+------------------+---------
 128 | relation      | accounts |      |       |     | RowExclusiveLock | t
 128 | transactionid |          |      |       | 858 | ExclusiveLock    | t
 142 | relation      | accounts |      |       |     | RowExclusiveLock | t
 142 | transactionid |          |      |       | 859 | ExclusiveLock    | t
 142 | transactionid |          |      |       | 858 | ShareLock        | f
 142 | tuple         | accounts |    0 |     1 |     | ExclusiveLock    | t

 pid | blocked_by | wait_event_type |  wait_event
-----+------------+-----------------+---------------
 142 | {128}      | Lock            | transactionid
```

Each transaction holds an ExclusiveLock on its own id. Terminal 2 found 858 in the row's `t_xmax`, so it asks for a ShareLock on transaction 858, which it gets only when 858 ends: `granted = f`. The `tuple` lock on `(0,1)` is its place in line for the row. Both hold RowExclusiveLock on the table, the mode every UPDATE takes; it doesn't conflict with itself, which is why two UPDATEs of different rows never wait for each other. When terminal 1 commits, terminal 2's UPDATE returns at once. Your pids and ids differ.

sections.h: Locks are held until commit: two-phase locking
sections.body:
When should a transaction let go of a lock? The obvious answer is as soon as it's done with the row. Take transfer A: it debits account 1, releases the lock, then credits account 2. Between those two steps, refund B locks account 1 and writes its change on top of A's debit. Then A fails on account 2, a timeout or a broken check, and rolls back. Undoing A's debit would wipe out B's change too, because B built on it. B used a value that, as it turns out, never existed, and B may already have committed.

The rule that prevents this is **two-phase locking** (2PL). A transaction takes locks while it runs, the growing phase, and starts giving them up only once it will take no more, the shrinking phase. It never takes a lock after releasing one. If every transaction follows the rule and locks everything it reads and writes, the outcome equals some serial order of the transactions. PostgreSQL, InnoDB and Oracle use the strict form for row locks: a transaction holds every lock until COMMIT or ROLLBACK and then releases all of them at once, so nobody can build on a change that might still be rolled back. In the lab, that moment is `release(tx)`.

Strict 2PL explains the most common lock outage in production, because tables have locks too. Every SELECT takes an ACCESS SHARE lock on the table, which conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Both are held to the end of the transaction. So a migration that runs `ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN note text` waits for every open transaction that has touched `accounts`, including one that ran a SELECT and has sat `idle in transaction` since. That alone is fine. The queue is the problem: every query that arrives after the ALTER waits behind it, even a plain SELECT that is compatible with every lock already granted. One forgotten transaction plus one migration stops all traffic to the table. In the Try it, a one-row SELECT waits with `blocked_by` pointing at the ALTER, not at the open transaction.

The fix is to let the migration give up instead of queueing: run `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` before the ALTER and retry it later. The statement fails with `canceling statement due to lock timeout`, and the queue behind it moves again.

try.title: Watch a migration block every reader
steps: Open a third terminal in `labs/` and run the same psql command.
Terminal 1: read `accounts` in a transaction and leave it open. Terminal 2: run the ALTER. Terminal 3: read one row. Predict which of the three return.
Terminal 1: list the table's locks, then commit and watch terminals 2 and 3. Repeat with `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` in terminal 2 and a second ALTER, while terminal 1 holds a transaction open again.

code.title: three psql sessions

try.expect:
While terminal 1's transaction is open:

```text
 pid |        mode         | granted | blocked_by
-----+---------------------+---------+------------
 176 | AccessShareLock     | t       | {}
 166 | AccessExclusiveLock | f       | {176}
 173 | AccessShareLock     | f       | {166}
```

Pid 176 is terminal 1, 166 the ALTER and 173 the one-row SELECT. The SELECT asks for AccessShareLock, which is compatible with the only granted lock, and still waits: it is blocked by the ALTER queued ahead of it. When terminal 1 commits, the ALTER runs, then the SELECT returns `customer`. With `lock_timeout` set, the second ALTER gives up after 2 seconds instead of holding the line:

```text
ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
```

Your pids differ.

sections.h: A deadlock is a cycle of waits, and one transaction has to lose
sections.body:
Locks bring a new way to fail. Transfer A moves 12 euros from account 1 to account 2 while transfer B moves 8 euros from account 2 to account 1. A locks account 1 and B locks account 2. Then A asks for account 2 and waits for B, and B asks for account 1 and waits for A. Neither can ever move on, and strict 2PL forbids either from letting go early. That is a **deadlock**. Make one in the simulator: you are the scheduler.

There are two ways out: prevent deadlocks or detect them. To prevent them, every transaction takes its locks in one global order, say lowest account id first. The transfer from 2 to 1 then locks account 1 first, waits for A there, and holds nothing A needs. That is the right fix in your own code, and the PostgreSQL docs give the same advice. A database can't impose it, because it can't know which rows your next statement will touch.

So the database detects them. It draws a **waits-for graph**: one node per transaction, and an edge from each waiting transaction to each transaction it waits for. That includes one queued ahead of it in the same line, as the figure's T3 shows. A chain, C waiting for B waiting for A, ends by itself: A finishes, then B, then C. A cycle never does. Finding one is a depth-first search that follows edges until it comes back to a transaction already on its path. The database then picks a victim, aborts it, releases its locks, and the others carry on. The lab picks the youngest transaction on the cycle, the highest id, which has probably done the least work.

PostgreSQL doesn't search on every wait, because the search is expensive and most waits end quickly. A waiting backend sets a timer of `deadlock_timeout`, 1 second by default. When it fires, that backend searches the graph, and if it finds a cycle through itself it usually aborts its own transaction, with `ERROR: deadlock detected`, SQLSTATE 40P01. The docs warn that which transaction loses is hard to predict. In the Try it, terminal 1 waited first, but its check ran before terminal 2 closed the cycle, so terminal 2's check found it and terminal 2 lost.

Under load, a deadlock is a normal outcome, like a serialization failure. The application retries the losing transaction from the start.

sim.title: Two transfers lock the same two rows
sim.intro: You are the scheduler. Tx A moves 12 from account 1 to account 2; Tx B moves 8 from account 2 to account 1. Each UPDATE locks its row until COMMIT. First make both get stuck. Then reset and get both to commit, with account 1 at 996.

steps.code: UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 1   -- locks row 1
UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 2   -- locks row 2
UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 2   -- locks row 2
UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 1   -- locks row 1

goal.say: Both committed: account 1 lost 12 and got 8 back. Whoever reached a row second waited there, and nothing was lost. When you ran the two first UPDATEs before either second one, each held the row the other needed: that cycle is the deadlock PostgreSQL breaks by aborting one transaction.

try.title: Make PostgreSQL break a deadlock
steps: Terminal 1: begin transfer A and debit account 1. Terminal 2: begin transfer B and debit account 2.
Terminal 1: credit account 2; it waits. Wait a couple of seconds, then in terminal 2 credit account 1. Predict which terminal gets an error, and when.
Commit in both terminals and read the balances.

code.title: two psql sessions

try.expect:
About a second after terminal 2's second UPDATE, terminal 2 gets:

```text
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 246 waits for ShareLock on transaction 870; blocked by process 249.
Process 249 waits for ShareLock on transaction 871; blocked by process 246.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,4) in relation "accounts"
```

and at the same moment terminal 1's UPDATE returns. Terminal 2's COMMIT answers `ROLLBACK`, because its transaction was aborted. The balances show A's transfer and nothing of B's:

```text
 id | balance_cents
----+---------------
  1 |         98800
  2 |         21200
```

The DETAIL lines are the cycle in the waits-for graph: each process waits for the other's transaction. Your pids and ids differ. If you wait more than a second between the two second UPDATEs, terminal 2 loses, as here; run them within a second and either may lose.

sections.h: Serializable snapshot isolation catches what row locks miss
sections.body:
Row locks order the writers of one row. They can't see write skew, the anomaly lesson 7's lab left passing. Account acct-17 has two cards with 75 euros each, and the rule is that the account's total must not go below zero. Withdrawal A checks the total, 150, and takes 100 from card 1. Withdrawal B checks the total, 150, and takes 100 from card 2. They write different rows, so no row lock and no `t_xmax` ever conflict. Both commit and the total is -50. Run one after the other, the second would have seen 50 and refused.

Version 1 makes reads lock too. Under strict 2PL every row a transaction reads gets an S lock, held until commit. A's S locks on both cards block B's X lock on card 2, and B's block A's on card 1, so they deadlock and one is retried. That is correct, and it is how MySQL's InnoDB implements SERIALIZABLE: with autocommit off, it turns plain SELECTs into `SELECT ... FOR SHARE`. But it brings back what MVCC removed. Lesson 7's month-end report would lock 2 million rows and stall every transfer. And a third card inserted during the check would slip past row locks, so the database must also lock ranges of keys.

Version 2 is **serializable snapshot isolation** (SSI), PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level since 9.1. Transactions keep their snapshots and never wait to read. Each read leaves a note, an SIREAD lock, saying "this transaction read this row", or this page, or the whole table after a sequential scan. A note blocks nothing. When a transaction writes a version that a concurrent transaction read, PostgreSQL records a read-write dependency from the reader to the writer. The reader didn't see that write, so in any serial order that explains what happened, the reader must come first. In the cards example, B read card 1 before A changed it, so B must come before A. A read card 2 before B changed it, so A must come before B. Both can't be true.

Searching the whole graph for cycles after every write would be slow. The theory behind SSI, from Alan Fekete and colleagues, shows that every such cycle contains two read-write edges in a row, T1 to T2 to T3, where T3 is the first to commit. So PostgreSQL only watches for a transaction with a read-write edge coming in and another going out, a **pivot**, and aborts one transaction of the pattern with SQLSTATE 40001. The stepper follows the cards. The pattern can appear without a real cycle, and coarse SIREAD locks make that more likely, so SSI has false positives. Under SERIALIZABLE every transaction needs a retry loop. In exchange you get correctness without analysing every pair of transactions yourself, and PostgreSQL's authors measured a cost under 7% compared with snapshot isolation on their benchmarks.

But now A must come before B and B before A, which no serial order can do. Each transaction has a read-write edge coming in and one going out: each is a **pivot**, the pattern the theory says every anomaly contains.

In the theory's terms A is T3, the first to commit,</text><text class="t-s" x="16" y="288" text-anchor="start">and B is the pivot whose outgoing edge points at it.</text></svg>
frames.say: A commits first. PostgreSQL lets it: aborting A now would not help B anyway. B is the pivot of a dangerous structure whose transaction on the far side, A, has committed, so B can no longer commit safely.

Its write to card 2 is rolled back. Total: 50.</text></svg>
frames.say: B's COMMIT fails with `could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`, SQLSTATE 40001, reason "identification as a pivot, during commit attempt". B's new version of card 2 belongs to an aborted transaction, so nobody will ever see it. The total is 50, as if A had run alone.

Its new snapshot sees A's</text><text class="t-s" x="16" y="288" text-anchor="start">withdrawal: 50 is less than 100, so B refuses. Same result as A, then B.</text></svg>
frames.say: The application's retry loop runs B again from the start. Its new snapshot includes A's commit, the total is 50, and B refuses the withdrawal. The end state equals running A, then B, one after the other, which is the promise SERIALIZABLE makes.

try.title: Get a serialization failure
steps: Run the block below in the order of its comments. Predict: does either UPDATE wait? Which COMMIT fails?
Then run it once more with `REPEATABLE READ` instead of `SERIALIZABLE` in both terminals, after resetting the cards with `UPDATE cards SET balance_cents = 7500;`. Predict the final balances.

code.title: two psql sessions

try.expect:
With REPEATABLE READ both commit and both cards end at -2,500: the account is 50 euros overdrawn. With SERIALIZABLE, both reads return 15,000, both UPDATEs succeed without waiting, and terminal 2 sees the SIREAD notes:

```text
 locktype |    rel     | page |    mode    | pid
----------+------------+------+------------+-----
 page     | cards_pkey |    1 | SIReadLock | 287
 relation | cards      |      | SIReadLock | 287
 page     | cards_pkey |    1 | SIReadLock | 297
 relation | cards      |      | SIReadLock | 297
```

Terminal 1's COMMIT succeeds. Terminal 2's fails:

```text
ERROR:  40001: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.

 id | balance_cents
----+---------------
  1 |         -2500
  2 |          7500
```

(LOCATION line trimmed.) The sum read the whole table with a sequential scan, so each transaction holds a SIREAD lock on the table `cards`, plus one on the index page its UPDATE searched. Only one withdrawal happened, and a retry of terminal 2's would now see a total of 50 euros and refuse. Your pids differ. When you are done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

refs.title: Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL (VLDB 2012)

analogy: A lock manager works like the reference desk of a library. Several readers can study the same rare book at once (shared), but the conservator who wants to rebind it needs it alone (exclusive), and once she is waiting, readers who arrive later queue behind her so she isn't kept waiting all day. Strict two-phase locking is the house rule that you hand back every book only when you leave the building. A deadlock is two readers each holding a volume the other needs before they can finish. The analogy breaks there: people would notice and one would step aside, while a database only finds out by drawing the waits-for graph, and then it throws one reader out and makes them start their research over.
in_your_world: Most deadlocks in payment services come from transfers and refunds that touch the same two accounts in different orders. Lock the rows in a fixed order (`SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id IN (:a, :b) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`, then the updates) and those deadlocks disappear. Oracle detects deadlocks automatically too and raises ORA-00060; its SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, so it allows write skew. In PostgreSQL, if you choose SERIALIZABLE for a ledger, wrap each transaction in a retry loop on SQLSTATE 40001 and 40P01 (in Quarkus, a retry policy around the `@Transactional` method, or a Temporal activity retry that re-runs the whole unit). Don't retry inside the failed transaction: it is dead. For job queues, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets workers take rows nobody else has locked instead of queueing behind each other, and every schema migration in CI/CD should set `lock_timeout`.
mistake: The common mistake is believing MVCC means no locks, and then reaching for SERIALIZABLE, or for nothing, without a retry loop. A team sees `could not serialize access` or `deadlock detected` in the logs, treats it as a database bug, and either drops back to READ COMMITTED, which silently lets write skew through, or catches the exception and carries on, losing the payment. Both errors are the database working as designed: it aborted a transaction to keep the result equal to some serial order. The fix is to make every transaction safe to retry from the start (idempotency keys help), retry on SQLSTATE 40001 and 40P01 a few times with a short jittered backoff, and keep transactions short so conflicts stay rare.

compare.title: Two ways to make transactions serializable

a.label: Strict 2PL
a.title: MySQL InnoDB SERIALIZABLE, autocommit off
a.src:
A: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- S locks card 1, card 2
B: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- S locks card 1, card 2
A: UPDATE card 1                -- needs X: waits for B's S
B: UPDATE card 2                -- needs X: waits for A's S
   -> deadlock: one is aborted, the other commits

readers block writers: yes
phantoms: blocked by locks on key ranges
failure: deadlock (or a lock wait timeout)

b.label: SSI
b.title: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE
b.src:
A: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- SIREAD notes, no blocking
B: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- SIREAD notes, no blocking
A: UPDATE card 1                -- edge B -> A, no wait
B: UPDATE card 2                -- edge A -> B, no wait
A: COMMIT                       -- ok
B: COMMIT                       -- 40001: pivot

readers block writers: no
phantoms: SIREAD notes on index pages
failure: serialization failure, sometimes false

compare.note: Both abort one of the two withdrawals, and both need a retry loop in the application. 2PL finds out by making the transactions wait for each other until they deadlock, and every reader on the way blocks writers. SSI lets everything run, records who read what, and aborts at the pattern every anomaly must contain, at the price of an occasional abort that wasn't strictly needed.

worked.title: Find the deadlock in a lock table

steps.say: Four transactions and two rows. Read the queues: granted requests first, then waiters in arrival order. Each transaction waits for at most one lock.
steps.code:
acct-1:  T1 X (granted)        | T2 X, T4 S waiting
acct-2:  T2 S, T3 S (granted)  | T1 X waiting

steps.say: Draw the waits-for edges: each waiter to every other request ahead of it in its queue whose mode conflicts with its own. T4's S request conflicts with T1's X and with T2's waiting X, so T4 has two edges. T1 conflicts with both S holders of acct-2.
steps.code:
T2 -> T1            (acct-1: the holder)
T4 -> T1, T2        (acct-1: the holder and the waiter ahead)
T1 -> T2, T3        (acct-2: both S holders)

steps.say: Search depth-first from the lowest id, following edges in increasing order. From T1 go to T2; from T2 the only edge goes back to T1, which is on the path: a cycle.

Pick the victim: the youngest on the cycle, T2, not T4, which waits on the cycle but isn't on it. Aborting T2 removes its S on acct-2 and its waiting X on acct-1. T1 now gets acct-2 once T3 releases it, which is a chain, not a cycle, and T4 gets acct-1 after T1. Nobody else has to die.
steps.code:
victim = cycle.max() = T2
after abort(T2):
  acct-1:  T1 X  | T4 S waiting            T4 -> T1
  acct-2:  T3 S  | T1 X waiting            T1 -> T3
no cycle: T3 commits, then T1, then T4

lab.title: Build a lock manager with deadlock detection
steps: Read the class comment of `LockManager.kt`: the queue rules, upgrades, and how `acquire` answers true or false instead of blocking a thread. Then read the provided `grantWaiters`.
Run the tests once. All 14 fail.
Write `acquire`, then `release` (remove the transaction's requests and call `grantWaiters`). The tests about compatibility, queue order, fairness and upgrades pass.
Write `waitsFor` and `findCycle`. Check them against the graph test and the chain test.
Write `detectDeadlocks`, and run the tests until all 14 pass.
hints: A new request is granted when `q.all { it.granted && compatible(it.mode, mode) }`: that one test covers both "compatible with every holder" and "nobody waiting ahead".

For an upgrade from S to X while others hold S, insert the waiting X request at index `q.count { it.granted }`, right after the granted requests, so it goes ahead of other waiters. `grantWaiters` already merges it into the S request when it is granted.

In `waitsFor`, look at every entry before the waiter in its queue, granted or not, skip the waiter's own transaction, and add an edge when the modes conflict. The T3 in the figure, waiting behind another waiter, needs that.
In `findCycle`, keep the current path as a list: when an edge leads to a transaction already on the path, the cycle is the part of the path from that transaction to the end.

drill.title: Write deadlock detection from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given `waitsFor(): Map<Long, Set<Long>>` and `abort(tx)`, write `findCycle()` (a depth-first search that returns the transactions on a cycle) and `detectDeadlocks()` (abort the youngest on each cycle until none is left). Then answer: why does aborting one transaction always break the cycle it is on?

recap: Under MVCC readers don't lock, but writers do: a shared lock (S) shares with S, an exclusive lock (X) shares with nothing. PostgreSQL keeps row locks in `t_xmax` and waits on the holder's transaction id.
A request waits if it conflicts with a holder or if anyone waits ahead of it, so one queued ALTER TABLE makes every later SELECT on that table wait. Set `lock_timeout` on migrations.
Strict two-phase locking holds every lock until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so nobody builds on a change that might be rolled back.
A deadlock is a cycle in the waits-for graph. PostgreSQL looks for one after `deadlock_timeout` (1 s) and aborts a transaction with 40P01; lock rows in a fixed order to avoid it.
SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL is SSI: reads leave non-blocking SIREAD notes, read-write dependencies are tracked, and a pivot with an edge in and an edge out is aborted with 40001.
Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, every transaction needs a retry loop from the start.

quiz.q: T1 holds a shared lock on row acct-9. T2 is waiting for an exclusive lock on it. T3 now asks for a shared lock on acct-9. What does a fair lock manager like the lab's do with T3?
options: Grant it at once, since S is compatible with T1's S
Make it wait behind T2, so that T2 isn't starved by a stream of readers
Abort T2 to let T3 in
Grant it and move T2 to the back of the queue
quiz.why: Granting T3 would be compatible with the current holder, but then T4, T5 and every later reader could also jump ahead, and T2 might wait forever. So a request waits whenever anyone is waiting ahead of it. This is the same rule that makes a plain SELECT wait behind a queued ALTER TABLE in PostgreSQL.

quiz.q: A transaction releases its lock on account 1 right after debiting it, then locks account 2 to credit it, and finally fails and rolls back. Meanwhile another transaction updated account 1 and committed. What went wrong?
options: Nothing: the rollback restores account 1 and keeps the other change
A deadlock, which the database resolves
The other transaction built on a debit that was rolled back; locks must be held until commit (strict two-phase locking)
A write-skew anomaly, which only SERIALIZABLE catches
quiz.why: Releasing a lock early lets other transactions see and build on a change that may still be undone. Rolling back the debit would then also erase or contradict the committed change. Strict 2PL avoids this by releasing everything only at COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Nothing here waits in a cycle, so it isn't a deadlock.

quiz.q: The waits-for graph has edges T1 -> T2, T2 -> T3, T3 -> T1 and T4 -> T1. Which transactions does the lab's detector abort?
options: T4, the youngest overall
All four
None: the detector only handles cycles of two
T3, the youngest on the cycle; T4 just waits for T1
quiz.why: Only T1, T2 and T3 form a cycle; T4 waits on it but isn't part of it, so aborting T4 would break nothing. Aborting T3 releases its locks and removes its waiting request, so T2 can proceed, then T1, then T4. Picking the highest id overall is the tempting mistake, and one of the lab's tests catches it.

quiz.q: Under PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE, a report runs `SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM settlements` for 20 seconds while 1,000 inserts into `settlements` commit. What happens to the inserts during those 20 seconds?
options: They run without waiting; SIREAD locks never block, though the report or a writer may later fail with 40001 if a dangerous pattern appears
They wait until the report commits, because the report's read locks block writers
They fail at once with 40001
They run, and the report sees each one as it commits
quiz.why: SSI's SIREAD locks only record what was read; the docs say they never block and can't cause a deadlock. The writers proceed, and the check for read-write dependencies decides at write or commit time whether someone must be aborted. Waiting for readers is what strict 2PL would do. The report never sees the inserts: it reads from its snapshot.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: two transactions under REPEATABLE READ update the same row. The first commits. What happens to the second, and what does lesson 8's lock manager add to that picture?
options: Both commit; the second overwrites the first
The second waits for the first (on its transaction id) and then fails with 40001; the waiting is the lock manager's queue, the failure is the snapshot rule
The second fails at once with a deadlock error
The second waits, then applies its change on top of the first
quiz.why: The first writer's id in `t_xmax` is the row lock, so the second writer waits for that transaction to end. Once it commits, a REPEATABLE READ transaction can't update a version it can't see, so it gets `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`. Applying on top of the new version is what READ COMMITTED does, which is the tempting answer.

flashcards.front: Which lock modes are compatible: S with S, S with X, X with X?
flashcards.back: Only S with S. An exclusive lock is compatible with nothing.

flashcards.front: Where does PostgreSQL keep a row lock, and what does a waiter wait on?
flashcards.back: In the row's `t_xmax`, as the locker's transaction id. The waiter waits for a ShareLock on that transaction id, which it gets when the transaction ends.
Take locks as you go and release all of them only at COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so nobody builds on a change that might be rolled back.

flashcards.front: Why can a plain SELECT wait behind an ALTER TABLE?
flashcards.back: The ALTER waits for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and the lock queue is fair: a later request waits behind anyone queued ahead with a conflicting mode.

flashcards.front: What is a deadlock, and how does PostgreSQL find one?
flashcards.back: A cycle in the waits-for graph. A backend that has waited `deadlock_timeout` (1 s) searches the graph and, on a cycle, usually aborts its own transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01.

flashcards.front: What is a pivot in SSI?
flashcards.back: A transaction with a read-write dependency coming in and another going out. Every serialization anomaly contains one, so PostgreSQL aborts when it sees one (SQLSTATE 40001).
No. They only record what a SERIALIZABLE transaction read, so writes to that data can be turned into read-write dependencies.

terms.plain: S lets other S holders in; X lets nobody else in. Reads that need stability take S, writes take X.
The component that records, per locked object, who holds it in which mode and who waits in line.
Never take a lock after releasing one. The strict form releases everything at commit or rollback.
Transactions waiting for each other in a cycle, so none can ever proceed.
A graph with an edge from each waiting transaction to each transaction it waits for; a cycle is a deadlock.
A non-blocking note that a SERIALIZABLE transaction read a row, page or table.
T1 read a version that a concurrent T2 then replaced, so T1 must come before T2 in any equivalent serial order.
Snapshot isolation plus tracking of read-write dependencies, aborting a transaction when a dangerous pattern appears.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks: "Our refunds run under SERIALIZABLE now and we see `could not serialize access` errors a few times an hour. Is PostgreSQL broken, and should we switch back to READ COMMITTED?" Explain what the error means and what to do.
explain_back.answer: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE runs every transaction on a snapshot and records what each one read, with SIREAD locks that never block. When one transaction writes something a concurrent one read, it records a read-write dependency between them. If a transaction ends up with such a dependency coming in and another going out, the transactions might not match any order of running them one at a time, so PostgreSQL aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001. It is the database keeping its promise, sometimes a little too carefully. Switching to READ COMMITTED would make the errors go away by letting anomalies like write skew through silently. The right fix is a retry loop that re-runs the whole refund transaction from the start on 40001, with idempotency keys so a retry can't refund twice, and short transactions so conflicts stay rare.

deeper.body:
**Soft edges.** PostgreSQL's lock manager README calls an edge to a holder a hard edge and an edge to someone queued ahead a soft edge. A cycle that contains soft edges can sometimes be broken by reordering the wait queue instead of aborting anyone; only a cycle of hard edges is a real deadlock. The lab aborts in both cases, which is simpler and still correct.

**Prevention with timestamps.** Instead of detecting cycles, some systems prevent them using transaction start times. Under wait-die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one, but a younger one that would wait for an older one aborts itself. Under wound-wait, an older transaction aborts (wounds) the younger holder instead of waiting. Either way, edges only point one direction in age, so no cycle can form; the price is aborts that a detector would not have needed.

**Optimistic concurrency control.** OCC takes no locks at all while a transaction runs: it records what it read, and at commit it validates that none of it changed, aborting if it did. That is what a `version` column with `UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND version = :v` does in your own code, and what JPA's `@Version` automates. It wins when conflicts are rare and loses when they are common, because every conflict costs a whole retry.

**Read-only transactions under SSI.** A transaction declared `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` waits at its start until it can get a snapshot that is guaranteed safe, then runs with no SIREAD bookkeeping and can never fail with 40001. It is a good fit for long reports. The PostgreSQL docs note it is the only case where SERIALIZABLE transactions block but REPEATABLE READ ones don't.

sources.title: Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL (PVLDB 5(12), 2012)
